This is not necessarily valid, since if population, income, and educational levels rise as a result of coal development, life styles of the Crows may change and the new jobs may be unable to keep up with demand. Any increase in the propensity of Crows to migrate from the reservation would seriously alter the analytical validity of these projected Crow population and income figures. It is also possible that the present high fertility rates will diminish in the future, reducing the natural increase factors utilized in this projection.
The non-Crow population's rate of natural increase is much lower. This population is also more subject to employment-induced migration, resulting in an irregular growth pattern. Figure III-5 illustrates the fluctuations which would occur under AF-2. The most significant changes occur in 1978 when the non-Crow population increases by 1586 (+26 percent), and between 1986 and 1989 when it decreases by 514 (-6 percent) over the 3 year period. These fluctuations do not occur under AF-1, which is more likely to be the case until at least 1980. The projected total non-Crow population change during the study period is 1872 (30 percent) increasing from 6098 in 1975 to 7969 in 2000.
Combining the non-Crow and Crow populations, total population changes from 10,000 in 1975 to 17,089 in 2000. The growth pattern for the impact area is predominantly a moderate, steady population increase. Within this pattern, however, there are a few rapid changes resulting from the migration of non-Crows.
